content: Awards are given to recipients, while degrees are formally conferred upon individuals who are then referred to as graduates. Alternatively, the individual is said to be admitted to a degree. A person may have a diploma, but a graduate is considered to be in a particular academic status. This distinction also explains why diploma studies can occur at either the undergraduate or advanced level, such as in programs like liceo classico, liceo scientifico, liceo linguistico, or perito tecnico. These programs may focus on fields such as physics, medicine, chemistry, engineering, or architecture. In modern university education, most courses are divided into two stages. The first degree, known as the laurea breve, is typically obtained after three years of study and the completion of a short thesis on a specific subject, such as particle physics or nuclear engineering. The second degree, the laurea magistrale, is awarded after the successful defense of a thesis, which often involves academic research or an internship within a private company. Only a small percentage of students continue their academic careers beyond this point, pursuing a dottorato (equivalent to a Ph.D.) after passing a public selection process. This advanced degree requires three additional years of study, primarily focused on research, supplemented by some mandatory coursework. The degree is conferred following the defense of a thesis based on the research conducted. Alternatively, after obtaining the laurea magistrale, individuals may choose to enroll in a Master program. These programs, offered by universities and private organizations, vary widely in subject matter, duration, and cost. In Italy, the cost of a one-year Master program can exceed the total fees paid for the preceding university education. These programs often include a final internship within a company. Norway Prior to 2003, the Norwegian higher education system included approximately 50 different degrees and corresponding educational programs. Many of these degrees had titles incorporating the Latin terms candidatus or candidata, with the second part of the title often reflecting the profession or field of training in Latin. These degrees were retired in 2003 as part of a reform to align the system with an international system. This reform, known as Kvalitetsreformen (The Quality Reform), was passed by the Norwegian Parliament (Stortinget) in 2001 and implemented during the 2003/2004 academic year. It introduced standardized periods of study and the titles Master and Bachelor (baccalaureus). The system distinguishes between a general Master's degree and a Master's degree in technology. The latter corresponds to the former sivilingeniør degree, which should not be confused with a degree specifically in civil engineering. The title sivilingeniør remains in use for new graduates, who may also choose to adopt the older title. Additionally, all pre-2001 doctoral degree titles were replaced with the title Philosophical Doctor degree, written as philosophiæ doctor (instead of the traditional doctor philosophiæ). The title dr. philos. is reserved for individuals who qualify for a doctoral degree without participating in an organized doctoral program. Poland In Poland, the higher education system closely resembles the German model.
